The ability to store substantial fat reserves in the tail serves as a critical buffer against seasonal variation in food availability, enabling individuals to survive periods of resource scarcity without experiencing severe physiological stress. As individuals approach the upper limits of their lifespan, they exhibit signs of reproductive senescence, including reduced clutch sizes and lower hatching success rates. The combination of delayed sexual maturation, modest annual reproductive output, and exceptional longevity positions the leopard gecko as a slow-paced, K-selected strategist within its ecological community.
